newsitem.title: USA: ADM, units targeted in European probe.
newsitem.headline: ADM, units targeted in European probe.

text.p: Archer Daniels Midland Co., which pleaded guilty to U.S. price-fixing charges and paid $100 million in fines last year, said Wednesday it is now the target of a probe in Europe.
ADM and several of its European subsidiaries are among the subjects of an anti-competitive practices investigation by the European Commission of the European Community, the company said.

The Decatur, Ill.-based agribusiness giant said in a statement that the Commission is probing the possible participation of major manufacturers in anticompetitive practices or agreements in certain markets for amino acids, including the feed additive lysine, in the European Union.
ADM said the European probe was in its early stages and the outcome could not be predicted.
ADM shares traded off 87.5 cents at $21 a share in late trading on the New York Stock Exchange.
Analysts said the European probe is another nagging concern for the company, which has put several lawsuits and the U.S. antitrust investigation behind it.
"It's disconcerting," said Dain Bosworth analyst Bonnie Wittenburg. "But I don't think this in and of itself is a big stock mover."

Given the fact that ADM pleaded guilty in the United States last year to charges of fixing prices of lysine and citric acid, the probe by the European Community likely did not come as a surprise, an agricultural analyst said.
"ADM and the rest of the industry has surely anticipated this," said John Schnittker, a consulting economist in Santa Barbara County, Calif., who specialises in agricultural issues.
While amino acids, including the feed additive lysine, are relatively small product lines for ADM, they are among its highest-margin products, analysts added.
ADM, a major grain and oilseed processor, also produces ethanol and high fructose corn syrup.

It was not immediate clear what action the European Community could take against ADM if it found evidence of price-fixing. But based on the actions taken by the U.S. Justice Department against ADM last year, analysts said they expected the European Community to levy fines against ADM if price-fixing were proved.
ADM pleaded guilty last year to fixing prices of lysine and citric acid and paid a record $100 million in fines.
The U.S. Justice Department probe also resulted in charges against Ajinomoto Co. Inc. and Kyowa Hakko Kogyo Co. Ltd. of Japan and Sewon America Inc..
ADM also settled a lawsuit last year in the United States brought by several of its customers. As part of that settlement, ADM agreed to pay the customers $25 million.
